title: Information Technology Governance Framework: A Practical Guide
summary: What an information technology governance framework is, how COBIT, ISO/IEC 38500, NIST CSF and ITIL differ, and how to choose and implement the right one.
body_markdown:
An information technology governance framework is the set of structures, decision rights, policies and measures that lets an organization's leaders direct how technology is used, and check that it delivers value at an acceptable level of risk. No single framework fits every company. COBIT 2019, ISO/IEC 38500, NIST CSF 2.0 and ITIL each cover a different part of the job, and most mature organizations combine two or three. We walk through what each one does, how they differ, and how to pick and roll one out.

## TL;DR


- An IT governance framework defines who decides, who is accountable, and how IT performance, risk and compliance are monitored. Day-to-day IT management happens beneath it.
- The main options differ by purpose: COBIT 2019 for enterprise-wide governance, ISO/IEC 38500 for board-level principles, NIST CSF 2.0 for cybersecurity risk, ITIL for service management, TOGAF for architecture.
- The "five domains" people search for usually refer to COBIT 2019: EDM, APO, BAI, DSS and MEA.
- Choose by size, industry, culture and maturity, then tailor or combine. Start small, assign owners, and measure.

## What an IT governance framework is and why organizations use one


IT governance is part of enterprise governance.[ISACA describes it](https://www.isaca.org/resources/isaca-journal/issues/2016/volume-5/holistic-it-governance-risk-management-security-and-privacy-needed-for-effective-implementation-and) as evaluating stakeholder needs, setting direction, and monitoring performance and compliance, with the aim of creating stakeholder value by balancing benefits, risk and resource use. A framework turns that idea into something you can operate: named roles, decision rights, policies, controls and metrics.


The current international standard,[ISO/IEC 38500:2024](https://cdn.standards.iteh.ai/samples/81684/61bc5f7eee154e2cad5dbdb72f95d208/ISO-IEC-38500-2024.pdf) , frames governance of IT as guidance for governing bodies on the responsible, innovative, sustainable and strategic use of IT, data and digital capabilities, so that the organization fulfils its purpose and meets stakeholder expectations. The[2015 edition](https://cdn.standards.iteh.ai/samples/62816/45eed59451ca494ab29119b4dc35fa96/ISO-IEC-38500-2015.pdf) spells out the practical benefits: meeting legal, regulatory and ethical obligations, realizing expected benefits from IT investments, allocating resources efficiently, and managing risks and opportunities.


In practice, organizations adopt a framework for reasons like these:


- **Strategic alignment.** Technology spending follows business goals instead of individual preferences.
- **Risk management.** Technology and cybersecurity risks are managed within agreed tolerances.
- **Accountability.**[Frameworks support auditability](https://zylo.com/blog/it-governance-framework) , meaning evidence that investments are actively directed and risks are handled within established thresholds.
- **Compliance.** Regulators, auditors and customers can see how controls are owned and monitored.
- **Performance.** Leaders get metrics instead of anecdotes.


For security and compliance teams there is one more reason. Customers increasingly ask how you govern technology and security before they sign, and the answers come through due diligence requests and security questionnaires. A clear framework makes those answers consistent and fast to give.


## Governance versus management: where the line sits


The most common confusion is between governing IT and managing it. A[literature review of COBIT](https://aisel.aisnet.org/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1262&context=amcis2014) draws on ISACA's definition: governance evaluates needs, sets direction and monitors, while management plans, builds, runs and monitors activities in line with that direction. An[older ISACA article](https://blog.dinamika.ac.id/erwin/files/2013/02/jpdf041-ITGovernanceandIts.pdf) puts it another way: governance concerns performing and transforming IT to meet present and future business demands, and management concerns supplying IT services and operating IT.


ISO/IEC 38500 formalizes this as an Evaluate, Direct, Monitor cycle,[as ITLawCo summarizes](https://itlawco.com/focus-areas/it-governance/it-governance-standards-and-frameworks/) . The board evaluates options, directs plans and policies, and monitors results. Management then executes. The 2024 edition adds that governance is distinct from management but occurs throughout the organization, so a good framework[clarifies decision-making and collaboration](https://cdn.standards.iteh.ai/samples/81684/61bc5f7eee154e2cad5dbdb72f95d208/ISO-IEC-38500-2024.pdf) beyond the IT department alone.


If you are preparing for a certification audit under one of the ISO standards, these[ISO certification best practices](https://adverbum.com/post/iso-certification-best-practices-for-compliance-managers) are a helpful companion for compliance managers.


### Information governance is a different discipline


People also search for "information governance framework", and it is not the same thing. A[peer-reviewed study](https://scholarspace.manoa.hawaii.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/c2353cf4-af60-449f-8529-12c32915f65a/content) describes information governance as governing the capture, valuation, storage, use, control, access, archiving and deletion of information across its lifecycle. IT governance, by contrast, aligns IT strategy with business objectives to derive value from IT investments. The two overlap, and you will usually need both, but they answer different questions: "how do we treat our information?" versus "how do we direct our technology?"


## Core components and principles


Frameworks differ in vocabulary, but the building blocks are similar.[Zylo lists](https://zylo.com/blog/it-governance-framework) policies, procedures, operational controls, and performance metrics or KPIs as the main components. Common pillars across frameworks include strategic alignment, risk management, resource optimization, performance measurement, compliance and defined accountability.


ISO/IEC 38500:2024 aligns with ISO 37000 and, according to the[ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 40 working group](https://committee.iso.org/sites/jtc1sc40/home/projects/wg-1/published-wg1/content-left-area/isoiec-sc-40-wg-1-develops-the-s/white-paper-on-the-differences-b.html) , defines six elements of a governance framework:


1. **Direction:** where technology should take the organization.
2. **Capability:** the people, skills and assets needed.
3. **Policy:** the rules that guide behavior.
4. **Delegation:** who is empowered to act.
5. **Performance:** how results are measured.
6. **Accountability:** who answers for outcomes.


The 2015 edition makes the accountability point plainly: individuals and groups should understand and accept their IT responsibilities, and those responsible for actions[should have the authority](https://cdn.standards.iteh.ai/samples/62816/45eed59451ca494ab29119b4dc35fa96/ISO-IEC-38500-2015.pdf) to perform them. A RACI chart that names an owner with no authority fails this test. We have written a deeper breakdown of these[six elements of IT governance](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/what-is-information-technology-governance) and the frameworks boards should use.


## The major frameworks compared


The frameworks differ by purpose and are not interchangeable. An[independent comparison](https://www.itil.org.uk/blog/itil-vs-cobit-vs-togaf) describes ITIL as service-management focused, COBIT as governance and control focused, and TOGAF as enterprise-architecture focused, and notes that organizations may combine them when their scopes complement one another.


Framework Primary purpose Best suited to


COBIT 2019 Enterprise-wide governance and management of information and technology Regulated entities, financial services, public sector


ISO/IEC 38500 Principle-based guidance for boards and governing bodies Any organization that needs board-level oversight of IT


NIST CSF 2.0 Voluntary cybersecurity risk management Organizations of all sizes, especially in the US


ITIL IT service management and operational discipline IT departments running services at scale


TOGAF 10 Enterprise architecture governance Organizations managing complex architecture change


CMMI Capability maturity Teams measuring and improving process maturity


FAIR Quantified risk analysis Risk teams that need financial estimates of loss


The summary above follows[ITLawCo's overview](https://itlawco.com/focus-areas/it-governance/it-governance-standards-and-frameworks/) of the major standards, and the point about ITIL and TOGAF matches[Zylo's description](https://zylo.com/blog/it-governance-framework) .


### COBIT 2019


COBIT 2019 is an enterprise-wide framework with governance and management objectives, design factors, metrics, maturity and assurance. It is[widely used by regulated entities](https://itlawco.com/focus-areas/it-governance/it-governance-standards-and-frameworks/) , state bodies and financial services firms. It is the most comprehensive option, and the one most often meant when someone asks about "the domains" of IT governance (more on that below).


### ISO/IEC 38500


This is the shortest and most conceptual of the group. It gives governing bodies principles and a model rather than a catalogue of controls. That makes it a good anchor for board conversations, and it pairs naturally with a more detailed framework underneath.


### NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0


NIST CSF 2.0 is[voluntary guidance](https://tsapps.nist.gov/publication/get_pdf.cfm?pub_id=957322) organized into six high-level functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. It is designed to help organizations of all sizes manage cybersecurity risks. The addition of Govern as its own function is a useful signal: cybersecurity governance now sits at the center of the framework instead of at its edge. If you want the background, see our explainers on[what NIST is and what compliance means](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/what-is-nist) and on[mapping CSF to 800-53](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/nist-cybersecurity-framework-800-53) .


Teams working under the EU's NIS2 directive can use[compliance software for NIS2](https://trustview.se/en/nis2-2) to track measures, risks and responsibilities against the cybersecurity governance requirements, which fits alongside a CSF 2.0 program.


### ITIL, TOGAF, CMMI and FAIR


ITIL keeps services reliable day to day. TOGAF governs architecture decisions so that systems fit together. CMMI gives you a maturity scale, and FAIR quantifies risk in financial terms. None of them replaces a governance framework on its own, but each fills a gap in one.


## The five domains of IT governance


The "five domains" people ask about are typically COBIT 2019's.[ISACA explains](https://www.isaca.org/resources/news-and-trends/industry-news/2020/using-cobit-2019-to-plan-and-execute-an-organization-transformation-strategy) that the 40 governance and management objectives are grouped into five domains:


1. **Evaluate, Direct and Monitor (EDM):** the governance domain, where the board sets direction.
2. **Align, Plan and Organize (APO):** strategy, architecture, budgets, risk and security planning.
3. **Build, Acquire and Implement (BAI):** delivering projects and changes.
4. **Deliver, Service and Support (DSS):** operations, incidents and security services.
5. **Monitor, Evaluate and Assess (MEA):** performance, conformance and assurance.


Other sources describe five "focus areas" of IT governance in different words, such as strategic alignment, value delivery, risk management, resource management and performance measurement. Those overlap with the pillars above, but they are not a formal standard. When a question names domains, check which framework it refers to.


## How to choose a framework


The guidance from[Griffith University's IT governance course materials](https://griffithuniversity.pressbooks.pub/infotech-governance-policy-ethics/chapter/module-1-it-governance-frameworks/) is that you should choose based on size, complexity, culture, industry and maturity, and that you may tailor or combine frameworks to fit. A practical way to apply it:


- **Start from your pressure.** If an auditor or regulator is the driver, COBIT or ISO-aligned controls give you the vocabulary. If customers' security teams are asking, NIST CSF 2.0 is the common reference in the US.
- **Match depth to maturity.** A company with no formal IT decision rights needs ISO/IEC 38500's principles and a clear owner map before it needs 40 COBIT objectives.
- **Use design factors.** COBIT 2019 offers[11 design factors](https://www.isaca.org/resources/news-and-trends/industry-news/2019/cobit-design-factors) , grouped as contextual, strategic and tactical, to tailor a governance system to your enterprise.
- **Combine on purpose.** Many organizations build what ITLawCo calls an integrated governance fabric:[ISO/IEC 38500 for board alignment, COBIT for governance machinery, and ITIL for operational service quality](https://itlawco.com/focus-areas/it-governance/it-governance-standards-and-frameworks/) .


If your main concern is risk rather than governance as a whole, our guide to[IT risk management frameworks](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/information-technology-risk-management-framework) walks through choosing one. For the wider picture of how governance, risk and compliance fit together, see our overview of[GRC](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/grc-governance-risk-compliance) .


## Implementing your framework step by step


Implementation, according to the[same Griffith materials](https://griffithuniversity.pressbooks.pub/infotech-governance-policy-ethics/chapter/module-1-it-governance-frameworks/) , requires defining scope and objectives, roles, processes, policies, monitoring, reporting, evaluation and continuous improvement. Successful programs also depend on leadership commitment, stakeholder involvement and clear communication. Here is how we would sequence it.


1. **Define scope and objectives.** Decide which business units, systems and data the framework covers, and write two or three outcomes you want, such as faster audit evidence or fewer unowned risks.
2. **Assign decision rights.** Name who evaluates, who directs and who monitors. Make sure each person has the authority that matches their responsibility.
3. **Write the policies.** Cover acceptable use, access, change, third-party risk and incident response, each with an owner and a review cycle.
4. **Map controls to the framework.** Link your existing controls to COBIT objectives or CSF 2.0 functions so that you see gaps, not just activity.
5. **Choose metrics.** Pick a small set of KPIs tied to the objectives from step 1, and report them to the same committee each quarter.
6. **Run a first assessment.** A[90-day risk assessment approach using ISO and NIST](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/risk-management-assessments) is a realistic first cycle.
7. **Review and improve.** Treat the framework as a living program. Adjust after incidents, audits and strategy changes.


Supporting structures matter as much as documents. Our piece on[effective governance structures](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/strengthen-compliance-with-effective-governance-structures) covers committees and reporting lines, and the[cybersecurity checklist for CISOs](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/cybersecurity-checklist-for-cisos-2026-resilience-guide) helps you test the security side.

## FAQ


### What are the main IT governance frameworks?


The most widely used are COBIT 2019 for enterprise-wide governance, ISO/IEC 38500 for board-level principles, NIST CSF 2.0 for cybersecurity risk, and ITIL for service management. TOGAF, CMMI and FAIR cover architecture, maturity and quantified risk. Most organizations combine two or three.


### What is the difference between IT governance and IT management?


Governance evaluates needs, sets direction and monitors performance and compliance. Management plans, builds, runs and monitors activities within that direction. Governance is owned by leadership and the board, while management is owned by IT and business managers.


### What are the five domains of IT governance?


Under COBIT 2019 they are Evaluate, Direct and Monitor; Align, Plan and Organize; Build, Acquire and Implement; Deliver, Service and Support; and Monitor, Evaluate and Assess. Other lists of five focus areas exist, so confirm which framework a source means.


### What is the difference between information governance and IT governance?


Information governance manages information across its lifecycle, from capture to deletion. IT governance aligns technology strategy with business goals to derive value from IT investments. Organizations typically need both.
